with_skill.expectation: Asks batched clarifying questions before publishing numbers, covering at least abuse pressure, region count, gateway/edge capability, and deadline or effort ceiling
Frames limits as identity/auth-scope x endpoint-class x account-override, treating the plan-to-limit mapping as a deliberate choice rather than the automatic default
States which identifier each tier is keyed on and changes it up the ladder (IP for anonymous callers, API key or org for paid tiers)

Structures the tier ladder so anonymous/free callers learn limits from headers, self-serve paid tiers get a documented exact-numbers table, and any enterprise tier gets a process rather than a public number
Cites a named platform precedent that accepts fixed window's flaw purely for simplicity in a low-stakes context (Sentry), and distinguishes that context from Ferroline's

Notes that token bucket and leaky bucket are an effort tie (both maintain one bucket per key, differing in intent, not implementation weight), so the simplicity argument does not favor fixed window over them
Conditions any promotion of the sliding-window option on adversarial or scraping pressure, naming its higher compute cost
Names the weighted-sharing trade: a deterministic guaranteed rate is given up to eliminate the fully-blocked-small-tenant cliff
Acknowledges the quota paradox knowingly: throttling reduces the throttled tenant's own availability even when spare capacity existed, and this is an accepted trade, not a hidden one
Specifies Retry-After as delay-seconds rather than HTTP-date, citing the client bug where an HTTP-date is parseInt-ed into NaN and triggers a retry storm
Retry guidance states the consequence for continuing to hammer while throttled, such as banning the integration
Presents the named override shapes (ticket-based with lead time, spend-based auto-promotion, plan-gated, time-boxed self-serve burst) and picks one deliberately

Ties the doubled support tickets to a measurement plan baselined from Corvana's own first month, covering per-tier 429 rate, the share of 429s retried inside the Retry-After window, limit-related tickets, and override-request volume, since no industry thresholds exist

without_skill.expectation: Asks batched clarifying questions before publishing numbers, covering at least abuse pressure, region count, gateway/edge capability, and deadline or effort ceiling
Rejects a single 300 req/min limit shared across REST and GraphQL: REST is metered by request counting and GraphQL by cost points, as two separately published models
Expresses the GraphQL limit as a budget of cost points per window with a published cost formula, not a request count
Publishes burst and sustained as two explicit numbers per tier, never one blended figure
Recommends token bucket as the default algorithm, mapping bucket depth to the burst number and refill rate to the sustained quota
Frames limits as identity/auth-scope x endpoint-class x account-override, treating the plan-to-limit mapping as a deliberate choice rather than the automatic default
States which identifier each tier is keyed on and changes it up the ladder (IP for anonymous callers, API key or org for paid tiers)
Carves expensive operations out of the general budget with per-endpoint-class limits instead of one account-wide number
States the geographic scope of the published limit (global vs per-region enforcement)
Labels the published numbers operational hints rather than an SLA, reserving in writing the right to lower limits for stability

Structures the tier ladder so anonymous/free callers learn limits from headers, self-serve paid tiers get a documented exact-numbers table, and any enterprise tier gets a process rather than a public number

Flags token bucket vs leaky bucket as a commonly inverted naming pair and requires the published policy to describe the behavior (whether idle time banks burst capacity) rather than rely on the algorithm name
Declines the fixed-window switch for this public developer API, confining fixed window to internal or low-stakes limits where the boundary flaw is harmless
Cites a named platform precedent that accepts fixed window's flaw purely for simplicity in a low-stakes context (Sentry), and distinguishes that context from Ferroline's

Notes that token bucket and leaky bucket are an effort tie (both maintain one bucket per key, differing in intent, not implementation weight), so the simplicity argument does not favor fixed window over them
Conditions any promotion of the sliding-window option on adversarial or scraping pressure, naming its higher compute cost
Names the weighted-sharing trade: a deterministic guaranteed rate is given up to eliminate the fully-blocked-small-tenant cliff

Distinguishes load shedding from rate limiting (it keys off overall system state, so a well-behaved tenant can still be shed) and requires the published policy to disclose this rather than overclaim fairness
Keeps internal fairness machinery (weights, deficit round robin, shedders) out of the published policy, documenting only externally observable effects
Acknowledges the quota paradox knowingly: throttling reduces the throttled tenant's own availability even when spare capacity existed, and this is an accepted trade, not a hidden one
Cites thin IETF adoption (GitHub and Stripe emit no IETF fields) and that the spec is a pre-RFC Internet-Draft
Names a re-promotion trigger for IETF-fields-alone: the draft reaching RFC status, or a second Tier-1 platform adopting it
Cites RateLimit-Policy's distinct value: it lets a well-behaved client self-throttle before its first 429, which the legacy trio cannot express
Cites named Tier-1 production adoption of both header families (Cloudflare) as traction evidence for the both-families option
States that headers are advisory hints, never guarantees: a remaining count does not promise that many successful calls
Weighs the 60% own-SDK traffic share when ranking: an audience you control at both ends weakens the legacy trio's compatibility argument, since the fleet can move in one SDK release
Replaces the 403 with HTTP 429 plus a Retry-After header on every REST throttle, no exceptions
Specifies Retry-After as delay-seconds rather than HTTP-date, citing the client bug where an HTTP-date is parseInt-ed into NaN and triggers a retry storm
Retry guidance states the consequence for continuing to hammer while throttled, such as banning the integration
States the precedence rule: Retry-After takes precedence over any reset time computed from limit-state headers
Applies the machine-readability gate: 100% of throttle responses must carry a machine-readable signal a documented client can branch on, and the undocumented 200 path currently fails it
Publishes retry expectations only, leaving client-side retry mechanics (backoff implementation, retry budgets, idempotency keys) to the idempotency-and-retry discipline
Rejects publishing a fixed public Enterprise number: self-serve tiers publish exact numbers, the top tier publishes a process
Presents the named override shapes (ticket-based with lead time, spend-based auto-promotion, plan-gated, time-boxed self-serve burst) and picks one deliberately
Specifies a lead time for increase requests, citing vendor precedent such as at least 6 weeks for large increases or 24-hour-minimum structured tickets
Names at least one limit dimension that no override touches, and says so in the policy
Reserves in writing the right to lower any granted override for platform stability
Flags persistent override-request volume per quarter as the signal that the published tiers are set too low
Scales notice to blast radius and applies a lead-time floor to the decrease, citing the 6-week vendor precedent as a symmetric floor
Rolls the tightening out via the observe (log without enforcement), baseline (enforce at a high ceiling), refine (tighten from observed data) sequence on live traffic
Reserves emergency reductions for platform stability in writing, so they are policy rather than surprise
Counters the part-of-the-contract framing: published limits are operational hints, not an SLA, and the policy says so
Considers a secondary abuse guard triggered by request shape as a complement to cutting every free caller's quota, with its existence and trigger shape documented
Produces a standing written change-notice policy that explains the reasons for changes, not just a one-off migration email
Names the portability trap motivating the plan-independent cap: a query written against a bigger plan's allowance instantly fails on a smaller-plan account
Recommends a debug affordance returning a per-field cost breakdown so integrators can understand why a query costs what it costs
Recommends a budget-introspection mechanism that costs nothing to query, so a client can check its remaining budget for free

Keeps structural query guards (depth ceilings, required pagination arguments, persisted queries) out of scope as schema design owned by the GraphQL API design discipline, while owning the pricing and budget policy
Treats the region multiplication as a real exploit vector, not a documentation nit
Flags the MSA language: a published limit cited in a contract as an SLA commitment without the policy saying it is one is a named failure mode, and published numbers are operational hints
Where a separate pre-production quota is kept, shapes it as an aggregate volume-and-scope cap against evaluation abuse, not a faster per-minute limiter

Treats any resulting tightening, such as enforcing 1,200 truly globally, as a limit change requiring notice scaled to blast radius or an observe-baseline-refine rollout, not a silent configuration fix

Ties the doubled support tickets to a measurement plan baselined from Corvana's own first month, covering per-tier 429 rate, the share of 429s retried inside the Retry-After window, limit-related tickets, and override-request volume, since no industry thresholds exist
